notes:
Task and constraints: Find the minimum number of deletions needed to make word1 and word2 equal.
Idea: Compute the longest common subsequence length with a two-dimensional dynamic-programming table, then subtract twice that length from the total length.
Technique and why it applies: Matching characters extend the common subsequence by one; otherwise the state takes the larger result from dropping a character from either word. All characters outside the shared subsequence must be deleted from their respective words.
Invariant: a[i][j] is the longest common subsequence length of the first i characters of word1 and first j characters of word2.
Edge cases: Empty strings are supported by the zero-initialized boundary row and column. The snippet has inconsistent tab/space indentation in a blank/comment region, which could matter if actual indentation bytes are malformed.
Complexity: The table has O(mn) states and constant work per state, so time and space are O(mn).

Task and constraints: Compute the minimum deletions required to make two strings identical.
Idea: Use rolling two-row dynamic programming to compute the longest common subsequence, then return m+n minus twice its length.
Technique and why it applies: Each pair of prefixes either extends the common subsequence when characters match or takes the best result from dropping one character. Two rows retain only the previous word1 prefix and the current row.
Invariant: dp[i%2][j] stores the common-subsequence length for the processed prefix of word1 and the first j characters of word2.
Edge cases: Empty inputs return the other string's length because the DP stays zero. The method does not modify either input string.
Complexity: Time is O(mn) for all prefix pairs, and rolling storage is O(n) auxiliary space.

Task and constraints: Return all points on the convex hull boundary, including points lying along straight hull edges.
Idea: Sort unique points and build lower and upper monotone chains using a cross-product orientation test.
Technique and why it applies: The cross product detects clockwise turns. Popping only when the cross product is negative preserves collinear boundary points, unlike the strict-convex-hull variant that removes them.
Invariant: lower and upper each contain a boundary chain in sorted traversal order, with no clockwise turn left in the chain.
Edge cases: Duplicate points are removed before hull construction. For all-collinear points, the final special-case slice avoids returning duplicated interior traversal points.
Complexity: Sorting costs O(n log n); each unique point is pushed and popped a constant number of times, so hull construction is O(n). Space is O(n).

Task and constraints: Validate a markup code string with one outer tag, matching nested tags, uppercase tag names of length 1–9, and supported CDATA sections.
Idea: Parse the string left to right using a stack of open tag names, with separate handling for opening tags, closing tags, and CDATA.
Technique and why it applies: Opening tags push names, closing tags must match the stack top, and ordinary text is allowed only while inside a tag. CDATA content is skipped until the next ]]> marker without interpreting its contents as markup.
Invariant: The stack contains currently open tags in nesting order; successful validation requires the stack to be empty at end.
Edge cases: The method indexes code[0] and code[-1], so an empty string raises an exception rather than returning False. It also requires the complete string to begin with '<' and end with '>'.
Complexity: Each character is scanned a constant number of times, giving O(n) time and O(n) stack space.

Task and constraints: Check whether code is valid under the restricted tag grammar, including nested tags and CDATA blocks.
Idea: Use recursive parser helpers for text, CDATA, tag names, tag content, and matching closing tags.
Technique and why it applies: validTag parses an opening tag, recursively consumes its content, then requires the exact matching closing tag. CDATA is consumed as opaque text, so tag-like content inside it does not affect nesting.
Invariant: Each successful validTag call returns the index immediately after a complete balanced tag element.
Edge cases: The final check requires the one outer element to consume the entire string. Tag names are constrained to uppercase A–Z and lengths 1–9; malformed or unterminated constructs return failure.
Complexity: Parsing scans text and tags across the input, yielding O(n) time in the normal parser flow and O(n) recursion/stack space for deeply nested tags.

Task and constraints: Add and subtract signed fractions in an expression and return the result in lowest terms.
Idea: Split the expression into signed fraction terms, compute a common denominator, add scaled numerators, and reduce by a greatest common divisor.
Technique and why it applies: Replacing '-' with '+-' makes each term separable. The common denominator allows numerator addition, and gcd reduction produces the normalized fraction.
Invariant: result is the sum of all numerators scaled to the common denominator lcm; gcd then reduces numerator and denominator together.
Edge cases: A zero result makes get_gcd(0,lcm) return lcm, reducing to 0/1. The implementation uses true division and int conversions while calculating LCM/scaling, which can introduce floating-point concerns for larger values.
Complexity: For t fraction terms, splitting and combining are O(t) aside from gcd/LCM arithmetic; recursive gcd subtraction can be slower than Euclid's modulo algorithm. Space is O(t) for parsed terms.

Task and constraints: Determine whether four points form a square.
Idea: Compute Manhattan distances between all six point pairs, sort them, and require four equal nonzero shorter distances and two equal longer distances.
Technique and why it applies: A square has four equal sides and two equal diagonals, so the code tests that pattern in the sorted distance list.
Invariant: d is the sorted collection of pairwise Manhattan distances between the four points.
Edge cases: Repeated points are rejected because the smallest distance must be positive. However, Manhattan distance is not Euclidean distance and does not reliably preserve square side/diagonal geometry, so the method can misclassify valid or invalid point sets.
Complexity: It computes six distances and sorts six values, so time and auxiliary space are O(1) for the fixed four-point input.

Task and constraints: Check whether four points are the vertices of a nondegenerate square.
Idea: Compute squared Euclidean distances for all six pairs and require exactly two distinct positive distances.
Technique and why it applies: A square has one repeated side-length-squared value and one repeated diagonal-length-squared value; the set-size test captures the two values, while rejecting zero rules out duplicate points.
Invariant: lookup contains every distinct squared pairwise distance among the four points.
Edge cases: The six pair distances are all included, so a valid square yields exactly two values with the diagonal larger than the side. The code checks only set size and nonzero distance; it does not explicitly verify that the larger value is twice the smaller, which can permit false positives for other four-point shapes.
Complexity: Only six distances are calculated, so time and space are O(1).

Task and constraints: Find the longest harmonious subsequence, whose maximum and minimum values differ by exactly one.
Idea: Count each value's frequency and compare its count with the frequencies of its immediate neighbors.
Technique and why it applies: A harmonious subsequence can contain only values x and x+1 (or x-1 and x). Summing the two frequencies gives the largest subsequence for that adjacent-value pair.
Invariant: counter[num] stores the frequency of num, and res is the largest valid adjacent-value frequency sum found.
Edge cases: The method returns zero if no adjacent integer values both occur. The code imports Counter before the class; the standalone empty-string literals around the import/method do not disable the function.
Complexity: Counting and checking each value take O(n) expected time and O(u) space for u distinct values.

Task and constraints: Return the length of the longest subsequence with maximum and minimum values differing by exactly one.
Idea: Build frequencies as values are scanned and update the answer whenever an adjacent integer has already been seen.
Technique and why it applies: For each num, the current frequency plus lookup[num-1] or lookup[num+1] gives the size of a harmonious subsequence using that pair of values. The best sum is retained.
Invariant: lookup contains counts for all values processed so far, and result is the best harmonious length discovered among processed adjacent pairs.
Edge cases: A list containing only one distinct value returns zero because no adjacent value pair exists. Duplicates increase the frequency and therefore the candidate length.
Complexity: Each element performs constant expected-time dictionary operations, giving O(n) time and O(u) auxiliary space.

Task and constraints: Find how many cells have the maximum value after a set of prefix rectangle increment operations.
Idea: If no operations occur, every cell remains tied; otherwise count the cells in the intersection of all operation rectangles.
Technique and why it applies: Each operation increments the top-left rectangle defined by its two dimensions. Cells incremented by every operation have the largest total, and their common region has dimensions min(op[0]) by min(op[1]).
Invariant: The minima across operation rows and columns describe the shared prefix rectangle.
Edge cases: The empty-operations case returns m*n. The code assumes each operation has two values and the initial dimensions are positive.
Complexity: With q operations, finding minima takes O(q) time and O(q) temporary space for the unzip tuples, aside from the result scalar.

Task and constraints: Count cells with the largest value after rectangular prefix increments.
Idea: Shrink the candidate shared region by taking the minimum row and column extent of every operation.
Technique and why it applies: The cells affected by all operations receive the maximum number of increments. Their count is the product of the smallest operation dimensions, or the original m*n when no operation shrinks the region.
Invariant: m and n represent the dimensions of the intersection of all processed increment rectangles.
Edge cases: An empty ops list leaves the original dimensions unchanged and returns m*n. Operation dimensions are assumed to be valid positive prefix sizes.
Complexity: The method processes each operation once, taking O(q) time and O(1) auxiliary space.

Task and constraints: Return restaurant names common to two lists with the smallest sum of their indices.
Idea: Build name-to-index maps for both lists, compute index sums for common names, then return all names tied at the minimum.
Technique and why it applies: A shared name's index sum measures the requested preference score. The two-pass minimum selection preserves all ties rather than returning only one name.
Invariant: common maps each shared restaurant name to its combined index, and minimum is the best combined index found in the final scan.
Edge cases: If there are no common names, the answer remains empty. The method prints 1 for every common name as a debug side effect; it does not affect the returned list.
Complexity: Building maps and scanning common names takes O(n+m) expected time and O(n+m) space.

Task and constraints: Find common restaurants whose index sum across two lists is minimal.
Idea: Map each name in list1 to its index, then scan list2 and track the smallest combined index plus all ties.
Technique and why it applies: For a common name at index j, lookup[s]+j is its score. A smaller score resets the result list, while an equal score appends another valid answer.
Invariant: min_sum is the best combined index seen so far, and result contains exactly the common names tied at that score.
Edge cases: The early break when j > min_sum is safe because later list2 indices cannot reduce the score. Duplicate restaurant names are not expected by the problem.
Complexity: Building the map and scanning list2 take O(n+m) expected time and O(n) auxiliary space.

Task and constraints: Count nonnegative integers from zero through n whose binary representations do not contain consecutive ones.
Idea: Use digit DP over the binary representation with state for position, tightness to n, leading zeros, and the previous bit.
Technique and why it applies: The recursion tries each allowed bit up to the current bound and skips a one when the previous bit is also one. Memoization reuses results for the same position and state flags.
Invariant: fun(i,last,tight,leading_zeros) counts valid completions of the remaining binary suffix under those prefix conditions.
Edge cases: The leading-zero flag ensures padding zeros do not affect the consecutive-one rule. The fixed dp array has 30 positions, which is sufficient only under the intended bound on n; larger bit lengths would index beyond it.
Complexity: There are O(B) positions and a constant number of states per position, giving O(B) time and space for bit width B, assuming the fixed array is large enough.

Task and constraints: Count integers in [0,num] whose binary representation has no consecutive one bits.
Idea: Precompute Fibonacci-like counts for valid bit strings, then scan num's bits from most significant to least significant.
Technique and why it applies: dp[i] counts valid bit patterns of length i. Whenever num has a one at bit i, all smaller prefixes that place zero there contribute dp[i]; if a previous bit was also one, the scan stops after correcting the overcount.
Invariant: result counts valid numbers strictly below the prefix represented so far, and prev_bit records whether the preceding bit of num was one.
Edge cases: The final +1 includes num itself if its binary representation is valid. If num contains consecutive ones, the break excludes num and the invalid higher-prefix continuation.
Complexity: Precomputation and bit scan each take O(B) time, with O(B) auxiliary space for the DP array.

Task and constraints: Determine whether n new flowers can be planted without placing flowers in adjacent plots.
Idea: Add empty sentinel plots at both ends and greedily plant whenever the current plot and both neighbors are empty.
Technique and why it applies: The sentinels simplify boundary checks. After planting at i, the algorithm skips two positions; otherwise it advances according to nearby occupied plots to avoid violating adjacency.
Invariant: could_plant counts successful placements made so far, and all placements preserve at least one empty plot between flowers.
Edge cases: n=0 returns True immediately because zero placements are required. The original flowerbed is copied into a padded list, so the input is not modified.
Complexity: Each index is visited at most once with occasional skips, giving O(n) time and O(n) space for the padded list.

Task and constraints: Check whether at least n flowers can be planted without adjacent flowers.
Idea: Scan the flowerbed and greedily plant at any zero whose immediate neighbors are empty or outside the array.
Technique and why it applies: A placement is safe exactly when both adjacent positions are empty. After planting, n decreases; reaching zero or below means enough placements have been made.
Invariant: Every flower inserted so far is nonadjacent to existing flowers, and n is the number of additional placements still needed.
Edge cases: The first and last positions use boundary checks instead of indexing outside the array. The code modifies flowerbed in place; n=0 returns True after the first iteration for a nonempty bed, but an empty bed would return False.
Complexity: One pass gives O(n) time and O(1) auxiliary space, with in-place updates.

Task and constraints: Group file paths that have identical file contents based on directory listings encoded in strings.
Idea: Parse each directory string into its directory name and file entries, then group full file paths by their extracted content.
Technique and why it applies: For each file token, the code separates the filename before '(' and content between '(' and ')'. Files sharing the same content key are duplicates if the group contains more than one path.
Invariant: files[content] stores every full path encountered with that content.
Edge cases: The parser assumes the standard format with a directory followed by space-separated filename(content) tokens. File contents containing spaces would not be parsed correctly by the simple split.
Complexity: For total input text length T, parsing and grouping take O(T) expected time and O(T) space for stored paths and content keys.

Task and constraints: Count triples of positive side lengths that can form a nondegenerate triangle.
Idea: Sort side lengths and use two pointers for each smallest side to count pairs whose sum exceeds the third side.
Technique and why it applies: For fixed i and j, if nums[i]+nums[j] exceeds nums[k], every index between j+1 and k-1 also forms a triangle with i and j because the array is sorted. The monotonic k pointer avoids restarting the search.
Invariant: For each fixed i and current j, k is the first index not satisfying the triangle inequality for that pair.
Edge cases: Zero-length sides are skipped. Sorting mutates nums, and duplicate side lengths are counted as distinct index choices.
Complexity: Sorting costs O(n log n), and the nested i,j loops with monotonic k give O(n²) time. Auxiliary space is O(1) beyond sorting implementation.
